newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Parliamentarian calls for pressure on Taleban.
newsitem.headline: Parliamentarian calls for pressure on Taleban.

text.p: A visiting German parliamentarian on Sunday accused the purist Islamic Taleban of running what he said was close to a "religious police state" and said the West should be cautious in recognising them as the legitimate government in Afghanistan.
Speaking in Kabul on Sunday evening, Ulrich Fischer of the Alliance 90/Greens party in the German Parliament, said he was worried about the fate of the intelligensia in Afghanistan.
"This is close to a religious police state. In the rural provinces the Taleban have brought security. That is an advantage and the lives of the people has not changed much." Fischer told Reuters.
"But we are anxious about the fate of city culture in Kabul, the only real city in Afghanistan. We have moved beyond ideology in this fight: it is the country against the city.
"A nation without an intelligensia is a dead place, it loses its political and cultural capacity," said Fischer.
Fischer is leading a delegation of five members of the party on a two-week fact-finding tour of Afghanistan.
"We should lobby the European Union to be very conservative in their official recognition of the Taleban." said Fischer.

In the 80 percent of the country the Taleban control they have imposed their strict vision of Islamic Law, banning women from the workplace and forcing them to wear the burqa, a shroud-like veil that leaves only a small patch of gauze over the eyes to see out of.
"I find this extreme interpretation of what they think of as Islam dangerous." he said. "The Taleban have a closed approach. They are not even open to talk about a more open interpretation."
However, Fischer advised continuing dialogue with the Taleban.

"I would like to continue to cooperate with this government until the situation is sorted out. But we would like the Taleban to not only talk about relaxing their curricula for women, we would also like them to do something about it."
Fischer said his party would be putting a motion before the German parliament calling on the government to put pressure on Afghanistan and Pakistan to modify the policies of the Taleban.
"The motion concentrates on the womens question. It calls on Germany to put pressure on Afghanistan and Pakistan."
He believed the Taleban was the brainchild of certain elements in Pakistan, but that they had ceased to direct Taleban policy.
"I believe that the the Taleban were formed by Pakistan, but I dont think they are steered by them," said Fischer. Both Pakistan and the Taleban deny there is any connection between them.

The Taleban have yet to be recognised as the legitimate authority in Afghanistan by any international body or nation. Fischer believes that the denial of recognition is another way to put pressure on the Taleban.
"Afghanistan cannot remain a white spot on the map forever. The Taleban want to be part of the world, they know that cannot afford to be left out." he said.
